This tutorial walks you through the process of setting up OpenPipeline on your system and processing an example dataset.
We do not assume any prior experience with Viash, Nextflow or single-cell analysis.

<!-- Add a link to a no-code Viash Hub guide? -->

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Prerequisites"}

**Environment**

macOS, Linux, or Windows with WSL2, Nextflow needs a Unix-like environment.
We use Python to inspect output but it is not required for running workflows.

**Hardware**

We use a small example dataset (~1000 cells) and runs are capped to 4 GB RAM so they should run on a laptop.
To try with real data you may require more resources.

**Experience**

We don't assume any prior experience with Viash, Nextflow or single-cell analysis but we do assume you are comfortable running commands in a terminal and installing software.
:::

## General setup {#sec-setup-nextflow-and-docker}

These instructions show how to set up an environment for running OpenPipeline workflows.
The main tools we require are [Nextflow](https://www.nextflow.io/) and [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) (or alternatives, see below).
Nextflow also requires a Java runtime.

### Java

Java 17+ is recommended (11 is the minimum).

::: {.panel-tabset}

### macOS

```bash
# install Homebrew (https://brew.sh) first, then:
brew install openjdk@17
```

### Ubuntu / Debian

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install openjdk-17-jdk unzip curl
```

### RHEL / Fedora

```bash
sudo yum install java-17-openjdk-devel unzip curl
```

### Arch

```bash
sudo pacman -Syy jdk17-openjdk unzip curl
```

### Windows

Use [WSL2](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install) with Ubuntu, then
follow the Ubuntu / Debian commands above.

:::

Check it is installed correctly by running `java -version`.

### Nextflow

Follow the instructions in the [Nextflow installation guide](https://docs.seqera.io/nextflow/install#install-nextflow) or run these commands:

```bash
curl -s https://get.nextflow.io | bash
chmod +x nextflow
mkdir -p $HOME/.local/bin/
mv nextflow $HOME/.local/bin/
nextflow info
```

### Docker

Install [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) (macOS/Windows) or Docker Engine (Linux).
Start it, then check `docker --version`.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Docker alternatives"}
If Docker is not available or you prefer to not to use it, you can instead use [Singularity](https://sylabs.io/singularity/)/[Apptainer](https://apptainer.org/) or [Podman](https://podman.io/).
In that case you need to swap the `-profile docker` flag in the commands below for `-profile singularity` or `-profile podman`.
:::

### Add Viash Hub

Finally, tell Nextflow how to locate workflows on Viash Hub:

```bash
mkdir -p "$HOME/.nextflow"
cat >> "$HOME/.nextflow/scm" <<'EOM'
providers.vsh.platform = "gitea"
providers.vsh.server = "packages.viash-hub.com"
EOM
```

## Example setup

These instructions are specific to the example in this tutorial.
You do not need to follow them if you plan to run OpenPipeline workflows on your own data.

### Create resource labels

To limit the resources used during the example runs we create a custom config file.
Every OpenPipeline component has an assigned resource label.
In this file, we override those labels to limit the CPU and memory used for each step instead of the default values.
See [Tune compute resources](../guides/tune-resources.qmd) for more information on how these labels work.

```bash
cat > /tmp/demo.config <<'EOF'
process {
  withLabel: lowcpu      { cpus = 2 }
  withLabel: midcpu      { cpus = 2 }
  withLabel: highcpu     { cpus = 2 }
  withLabel: lowmem      { memory = 4.GB }
  withLabel: midmem      { memory = 4.GB }
  withLabel: highmem     { memory = 4.GB }
  withLabel: veryhighmem { memory = 4.GB }
}
EOF
```

### Get the data

We use two small public PBMC samples, sequenced with different 10x chemistries, so they carry a technical batch effect for the pipeline to correct.
They come as ready-made MuDate (`.h5mu`) objects matching the output of an ingestion workflow, one per sample.

```bash
mkdir -p data && cd data
base="https://openpipelines-bio.s3.amazonaws.com/openpipeline_docs/data"
curl -O "$base/pbmc_1k_v2.h5mu"
curl -O "$base/pbmc_1k_v3.h5mu"
cd ..
```

Each file holds one sample's raw RNA counts.
Open both in Python with the [`mudata`](https://mudata.readthedocs.io/) package to see what's inside:

```bash
pip install 'mudata~=0.3.8' 'anndata~=0.12.16'   # matches openpipeline v4.2.0, needs Python >=3.11
for s in pbmc_1k_v2 pbmc_1k_v3; do
  echo "== $s =="
  python -c "import mudata; print(mudata.read_h5mu('data/$s.h5mu'))"
done
```

```
== pbmc_1k_v2 ==
MuData object with n_obs × n_vars = 996 × 33538
  var:  'gene_symbol', 'feature_types', 'genome'
  1 modality
    rna:  996 × 33538
      var:  'gene_symbol', 'feature_types', 'genome'
== pbmc_1k_v3 ==
MuData object with n_obs × n_vars = 1222 × 33538
  var:  'gene_symbol', 'feature_types', 'genome'
  1 modality
    rna:  1222 × 33538
      var:  'gene_symbol', 'feature_types', 'genome'
```

Each sample is a separate object with a single `rna` modaulity of raw counts (cells × genes) and gene metadata in `.var`.

## Process the samples

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Ingestion"}
To reduce the time and resources needed for this tutorial we have skipped the ingestion step and provided pre-ingested `.h5mu` files.
See [Ingest data](../guides/ingest-10x.qmd) for instructions on how to run the ingestion workflow yourself.
:::

The `multiomics/process_samples` workflow filters low-quality cells from each sample, then concatenates the samples and performs normalization, highly variable gene selection, PCA, neighborhood graph calculation and UMAP.

We create a paramters file containing the setting we want to use.
Parameters can also be passed directly to the `nextflow run` command but a file is more flexible and provides a record of what was run.

```bash
cat > /tmp/params_process.yaml <<'EOF'
param_list:
  - id: pbmc_1k_v2
    input: data/pbmc_1k_v2.h5mu
  - id: pbmc_1k_v3
    input: data/pbmc_1k_v3.h5mu
rna_min_counts: 500           # thresholds you'd normally read off a QC report
rna_min_genes_per_cell: 200
max_fraction_mito: 0.2
output: pbmc_processed.h5mu
publish_dir: results/processed
EOF

```
Each entry in `param_list` is one sample.
The the `id` field provides a name and the `input` points at the file to process.
The remaining fields are global parameters applied to all samples.
If we wanted to use different thresholds for each sample we could add them to the individual entries in `param_list` instead of the global section.
The [Process many samples](../guides/process-many-samples.qmd) guide covers the full `param_list` model, and [Generate a QC report](../guides/qc-report.qmd) covers choosing the thresholds.


We then run the workflow with these parameters.
Notice that we specify a specific version of OpenPipeline (`-r v4.2.0`) to ensure reproducibility.

```bash
nextflow run https://packages.viash-hub.com/vsh/openpipeline.git \
  -r v4.2.0 \
  -latest -profile docker \
  -main-script target/nextflow/workflows/multiomics/process_samples/main.nf \
  -params-file /tmp/params_process.yaml \
  -c /tmp/demo.config
```

Inspect the result to see what processing added:

```bash
python -c "import mudata; print(mudata.read_h5mu('results/processed/pbmc_processed.h5mu'))"
```

```
MuData object with n_obs × n_vars = 2171 × 33538
  var:  'genome', 'filter_with_counts', 'gene_symbol', 'feature_types', 'filter_with_hvg', 'obs_mean', 'log1p_obs_mean', 'total_counts', 'log1p_total_counts', 'num_nonzero_obs', 'pct_dropout'
  1 modality
    rna:        2171 × 33538
      obs:      'filter_with_scrublet', 'filter_with_counts', 'scrublet_doublet_score', 'sample_id', 'num_nonzero_vars', 'log1p_num_nonzero_vars', 'total_counts', 'log1p_total_counts', 'pct_of_counts_in_top_50_vars', 'pct_of_counts_in_top_100_vars', 'pct_of_counts_in_top_200_vars', 'pct_of_counts_in_top_500_vars'
      var:      'genome', 'filter_with_counts', 'gene_symbol', 'feature_types', 'filter_with_hvg', 'obs_mean', 'log1p_obs_mean', 'total_counts', 'log1p_total_counts', 'num_nonzero_obs', 'pct_dropout'
      uns:      'log1p', 'neighbors', 'pca_variance'
      obsm:     'X_pca', 'X_umap'
      varm:     'pca_loadings'
      layers:   'log_normalized'
      obsp:     'connectivities', 'distances'
```

Low-quality cells have been removed and the two samples have been concatenated into a single object.
The `.obs["sample_id"]` column records which sample each cell came from.
We also added a range of other calculated values:

- Per-cell and per-gene QC metrics (`total_counts`, `pct_dropout`, `scrublet_doublet_score`, …)
- Normalized counts (`.layers['log_normalized']`)
- Highly variable genes (`filter_with_hvg`)
- PCA (`.obsm['X_pca']`) and UMAP (`.obsm['X_umap']`) embeddings
- A neighbor graph (`.obsp['connectivities']`, `.obsp['distances']`) built on the PCA embedding

## Integrate

These two samples contain a batch effect we want to correct before further analysis.
In this example we use the `integration/harmony_leiden` workflow but there are a range of other integration methods available in OpenPipeline, see [Integrate across samples](../guides/integrate.qmd) for details.

```bash
# Create a parameters file
cat > /tmp/params_integrate.yaml <<'EOF'
id: pbmc_integrated
input: results/processed/pbmc_processed.h5mu
obs_covariates: sample_id
output: pbmc_integrated.h5mu
publish_dir: results/integrated
EOF

# Run the integration workflow
nextflow run https://packages.viash-hub.com/vsh/openpipeline.git \
  -r v4.2.0 \
  -latest -profile docker \
  -main-script target/nextflow/workflows/integration/harmony_leiden/main.nf \
  -params-file /tmp/params_integrate.yaml \
  -c /tmp/demo.config
```

Inspect the integrated object the same way:

```bash
python -c "import mudata; print(mudata.read_h5mu('results/integrated/pbmc_integrated.h5mu'))"
```

```
MuData object with n_obs × n_vars = 2171 × 33538
  var:  'genome', 'filter_with_counts', 'gene_symbol', 'feature_types', 'filter_with_hvg', 'obs_mean', 'log1p_obs_mean', 'total_counts', 'log1p_total_counts', 'num_nonzero_obs', 'pct_dropout'
  1 modality
    rna:        2171 × 33538
      obs:      'filter_with_scrublet', 'filter_with_counts', 'scrublet_doublet_score', 'sample_id', 'num_nonzero_vars', 'log1p_num_nonzero_vars', 'total_counts', 'log1p_total_counts', 'pct_of_counts_in_top_50_vars', 'pct_of_counts_in_top_100_vars', 'pct_of_counts_in_top_200_vars', 'pct_of_counts_in_top_500_vars', 'harmony_integration_leiden_1.0'
      var:      'genome', 'filter_with_counts', 'gene_symbol', 'feature_types', 'filter_with_hvg', 'obs_mean', 'log1p_obs_mean', 'total_counts', 'log1p_total_counts', 'num_nonzero_obs', 'pct_dropout'
      uns:      'harmonypy_integration_neighbors', 'log1p', 'neighbors', 'pca_variance'
      obsm:     'X_leiden_harmony_umap', 'X_pca', 'X_pca_integrated', 'X_umap'
      varm:     'pca_loadings'
      layers:   'log_normalized'
      obsp:     'connectivities', 'distances', 'harmonypy_integration_connectivities', 'harmonypy_integration_distances'
```

Integration added the following fields:

- `.obsm['X_pca_integrated']`: the batch-corrected embedding (Harmony)
- `.obs['harmony_integration_leiden_1.0']`: cluster labels computed on that corrected embedding.
- `.obsm['X_leiden_harmony_umap']`: a UMAP of the corrected space
- `.obsp['harmonypy_integration_connectivities']` and `.obsp['harmonypy_integration_distances']`: a neighbor graph built on the corrected embedding

Assigning biological identities to the clusters can be done using an annotation workflow as described in [cell type annotation](../guides/annotate.qmd).
